children.translated_text: Now, the <s>Gauḍapādīya Kārikās</s> (verses of <s>Gauḍapāda</s>)
The one whose consciousness is directed outward is <s>Viśva</s>, the all-pervading;
the one whose consciousness is directed inward is <s>Taijasa</s>;
the one whose consciousness is condensed is <s>Prājña</s>—
it is one alone, regarded as threefold.
<s>Viśva</s> resides at the right eye,
<s>Taijasa</s> within the mind,
<s>Prājña</s> in the space within the heart—
thus it is established in three ways within the body.
<s>Viśva</s> always enjoys the gross,
<s>Taijasa</s> enjoys the subtle,
and <s>Prājña</s> enjoys bliss—
know that enjoyment is threefold.
The gross satisfies <s>Viśva</s>,
the subtle satisfies <s>Taijasa</s>,
and bliss likewise satisfies <s>Prājña</s>—
know that satisfaction is threefold.
In these three states, that which is to be enjoyed
and the enjoyer who is proclaimed—
one who knows both of these,
though enjoying, is not tainted.
The origin of all beings—
this is the settled conclusion regarding existing things.
<s>Prāṇa</s> (vital breath) generates everything;
<s>Puruṣa</s> (the Person) projects the rays of consciousness separately.
Others who reflect on creation
consider it a manifestation of divine power;
yet others conceive creation as being of the nature of dream and <s>māyā</s> (illusion).
Creation is merely the will of the Lord—
thus hold those certain about creation.
Those who reflect on time consider
the production of beings to be from <s>kāla</s> (time).
Some say creation is for the purpose of enjoyment,
others say it is for sport.
This is the very nature of the divine—
what desire can there be for one whose desires are fulfilled?
The Lord who brings about the cessation of all suffering,
the master, the imperishable,
the non-dual essence of all beings—
that God is known as <s>Turya</s> (the Fourth), the all-pervading.
<s>Viśva</s> and <s>Taijasa</s> are considered
bound by cause and effect;
<s>Prājña</s> is bound by cause alone—
but in <s>Turya</s>, neither of these two obtains.
<s>Prājña</s> cognizes neither the self nor others,
neither truth nor untruth—
<s>Prājña</s> cognizes nothing whatsoever.
<s>Turya</s>, however, is the ever-seeing of all.

children.text: na satyaṃ na api ca an-ṛtam

children.translated_text: The non-apprehension of duality is common
to both <s>Prājña</s> and <s>Turya</s>;
<s>Prājña</s> is possessed of seed-sleep (<s>bījanidrā</s>),
but that does not exist in <s>Turya</s>.
The first two (<s>Viśva</s> and <s>Taijasa</s>) are associated with dream and sleep;
<s>Prājña</s>, however, is with dreamless sleep.
Those who are resolute see in <s>Turya</s>
neither sleep nor dream.

children.text: na nidrāṃ na eva ca svapnaṃ

children.translated_text: Dream belongs to one who perceives wrongly;
sleep belongs to one who does not know the reality.
When the error regarding both is dispelled,
one attains the state of <s>Turīya</s> (the Fourth).
When the <s>jīva</s> (individual self), asleep due to beginningless <s>māyā</s> (illusion),
awakens,
then it realizes the unborn, sleepless, dreamless,
non-dual reality.
If the phenomenal world were real,
it would certainly cease to exist—no doubt about it.
This duality is nothing but <s>māyā</s> (illusion);
non-duality alone is the ultimate reality.
Conceptual differentiation would cease
if it were imagined by anyone;
this teaching is for the sake of instruction—
once reality is known, duality does not exist.
When one wishes to describe the identity of <s>Viśva</s> (with <s>Oṃkāra</s>),
the similarity at the beginning is prominent;
in the comprehension of the <s>mātrā</s> (syllabic measure),
the similarity of obtainment is likewise evident.
In understanding the u-sound as <s>Taijasa</s>,
the excellence is clearly seen;
in the comprehension of the <s>mātrā</s>,
the quality of being both is similarly evident.
When <s>Prājña</s> is identified with the m-sound,
the similarity of measure is prominent.
When there is non-apprehension of the <s>mātrās</s> (measures),
there is absorption into a state of commonality.
He who knows the sameness equally in the three states (<s>dhāmans</s>),
who knows the commonality with certainty,
he is worthy of worship by all beings,
and worthy of veneration — a great sage.
The letter 'a' leads one to <s>Viśva</s> (the waking state),
the letter 'u' likewise to <s>Taijasa</s> (the dream state),
and the letter 'm' again to <s>Prājña</s> (the deep sleep state);
in the measureless (<s>amātra</s>) there is no destination.
One should know <s>Oṃkāra</s> quarter by quarter;
the quarters are the <s>mātrās</s> (measures) — there is no doubt.
Having known <s>Oṃkāra</s> quarter by quarter,
one should not think of anything whatsoever.
One should concentrate the mind on <s>Praṇava</s>;
<s>Praṇava</s> is <s>Brahman</s>, free from fear.
For one who is perpetually united with <s>Praṇava</s>,
there is no fear anywhere.
<s>Praṇava</s> is indeed the lower <s>Brahman</s>,
and <s>Praṇava</s> is said to be the higher (<s>Brahman</s>).
Without prior cause, without interior, without exterior,
without successor — <s>Praṇava</s> is imperishable.
<s>Praṇava</s> is indeed the beginning of all,
the middle, and likewise the end.
Having known <s>Praṇava</s> in this way,
one attains that immediately.
One should know <s>Praṇava</s> as the Lord,
established in the heart of all.
Knowing <s>Oṃkāra</s> to be all-pervading,
the wise one does not grieve.
Without measure, of infinite measure,
the cessation of duality — auspicious (<s>Śiva</s>).
By whom <s>Oṃkāra</s> is known,
he is a <s>muni</s> (sage), and no other person.

children.text: col: iti (māṇḍūkyo1paniṣad-arthā3viṣ-karaṇa-parāyāṃ gauḍapādīya-kārikāyāṃ prathamam āgama-prakaraṇam [B:]gauda-pādīye āgama-śāstre āgamā3khyaṃ prathamaṃ prakaraṇaṃ samāptam)
children.translated_text: Colophon: Thus ends the first chapter called <s>Āgama-prakaraṇa</s> in the <s>Gauḍapādīya Kārikā</s>, which illuminates the meaning of the <s>Māṇḍūkyopaniṣad</s>.
Now begins the second chapter called <s>Vaitathya</s> (Unreality) in the <s>Gauḍapādīya Kārikā</s>.
The unreality of all entities
in dream, the wise declare,
because of the internal location of the objects,
and because of the reason that they are enclosed.
And because of the shortness of time,
upon waking one does not see those places visited;
and indeed everyone who has awakened
does not exist in that place.
The non-existence of chariots and the like
is declared through reasoning in scripture.
Thereby their unreality is established;
it is declared as manifested in dream.
Because of the internal location of the differences,
the same is considered true of the waking state.
As it is there (in waking), so in dream —
in being enclosed, they do not differ.
The wise declare that the states of dream and waking
are one,
because of the sameness of the differences (perceived in both),
for a well-established reason.
What does not exist at the beginning and at the end,
is likewise so in the present.
Though similar to the unreal,
they appear as though real.

children.text: ādāv ante ca yan na asti

children.translated_text: Their purposefulness
is contradicted in dream.
Therefore, because of having a beginning and an end,
they are indeed considered false.
Things with unprecedented properties,
as in the case of inhabitants of heaven —
he sees them, having gone there,
just as one well-trained here (sees familiar things).
Even within the experience of dream, internally,
what is imagined by the mind is unreal,
while what is grasped by the mind externally is real.
the illusoriness of both is established.
Even in the waking state, what is internally
imagined by the mind is unreal,
while what is externally grasped by the mind is real —
the illusoriness of both is reasonable.
If the illusoriness of both
the distinctions in both states is established,
who then cognizes these distinctions?
Who indeed is their imaginer?
<s>Ātman</s> (the Self) imagines Itself by Itself;
the Self, the luminous Lord, by Its own <s>māyā</s> (power of illusion).
It alone cognizes the distinctions —
this is the conclusion of <s>Vedānta</s>.
It projects the various objects
established (or unestablished) within the mind,
and those fixed externally in the mind —
thus the Lord imagines.
Those that are of momentary duration within the mind,
and those of dual duration externally —
all of them are merely imagined;
the distinction has no other cause.
Those that are unmanifest internally
and those that are clearly manifest externally —
all of them are merely imagined;
the distinction lies only in the difference of sense organs.
First It imagines the individual soul (<s>jīva</s>),
then the various objects,
both external and internal —
as one's knowledge, so is one's memory.
Just as a rope, undetermined
in darkness, is imagined
as a snake, a stream of water, and other things —
so too is <s>Ātman</s> imagined.
Just as when the rope is ascertained,
the false imagining ceases,
and there is the non-dual conviction 'it is only a rope' —
so too is the ascertainment of <s>Ātman</s>.
Through <s>prāṇa</s> (vital breath) and other infinite
entities, It has been imagined.
This is the <s>māyā</s> of that luminous Lord,
by which He Himself is deluded.
Those who know <s>prāṇa</s> call It '<s>prāṇa</s>';
those who know the elements call It 'the elements';
those who know the <s>guṇas</s> (qualities) call It 'the <s>guṇas</s>';
those who know the <s>tattvas</s> (principles) call It 'the <s>tattvas</s>'.
Those who know the <s>pādas</s> (quarters) call It 'the <s>pādas</s>';
those who know the objects call It 'the objects';
those who know the worlds call It 'the worlds';
those who know the <s>devas</s> (gods) call It 'the <s>devas</s>'.
Those who know the <s>Vedas</s> call It 'the <s>Vedas</s>';
those who know the sacrifices call It 'the sacrifices';
those who know the enjoyer call It 'the enjoyer';
those who know the enjoyed call It 'the enjoyed'.
Those who know the subtle call It 'the subtle';
those who know the gross call It 'the gross';
those who know form call It 'the formed';
those who know the formless call It 'the formless'.
Those who know time call It 'time';
those who know space call It 'space';
those who know disputations call It 'disputations';
those who know the worlds call It 'the worlds'.
Those who know mind call It 'mind';
those who know intellect call It 'intellect';
those who know consciousness call It 'consciousness';
those who know <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> call It 'these'.
Some say It consists of twenty-five principles;
others say twenty-six;
some declare It to be thirty-one;
others say It is infinite.
Those who know the worlds speak of worlds;
those who know the <s>āśramas</s> (stages of life) speak of <s>āśramas</s>;
those who know gender speak of female, male, and neuter;
others speak of the higher and the lower.
Those who know creation call It 'creation';
those who know dissolution call It 'dissolution';
those who know maintenance call It 'maintenance' —
all these views persist at all times.
Whatever nature one reveals to a person,
that nature that person sees.
That nature protects him, having become it,
and absorbed in it, he becomes identified with it.

children.text: taṃ ca avati sa bhūtva āsau

children.translated_text: Through these non-separate attributes,
It is characterized as if separate.
One who thus knows the truth
may imagine without hesitation.
Just as in dream and illusion are seen,
like a city of the <s>Gandharvas</s> (a mirage).
Thus this entire universe has been seen
by those well-versed in the <s>Vedānta</s>.
There is neither cessation nor origination,
neither one who is bound nor one who is a practitioner,
neither one who seeks liberation nor one who is indeed liberated—
this is the ultimate truth (<s>paramārthatā</s>).
This [<s>Ātman</s>] is imagined through unreal entities
and through the non-dual;
the entities themselves are [imagined] only through the non-dual—
therefore non-duality (<s>advayatā</s>) alone is auspicious (<s>śiva</s>).
This [world] does not come into being through the nature of another, nor through itself,
nor by itself in any way whatsoever;
nothing exists either separately or non-separately—
thus declare those who know the truth.
By sages who are free from attachment, fear, and anger,
who have mastered the <s>Vedas</s>,
this [reality] has been seen as free from conceptual distinctions (<s>nirvikalpa</s>),
the cessation of the phenomenal world (<s>prapañcopaśama</s>), non-dual.
Therefore, having known this thus,
one should fix one's mindfulness (<s>smṛti</s>) on non-duality;
having attained non-duality,
one should move in the world as if inert.
Without praise, without obeisance,
and even without the exclamation '<s>svadhā</s>,'
with both the moving and the unmoving as one's abode—
such a <s>yati</s> (renunciant) should be one who lives by chance.
Having seen the truth inwardly (<s>ādhyātmika</s>),
and having seen the truth externally,
having become one with the truth, delighting in the truth,
one should never deviate from the truth.

children.text: atha gauḍapādīya-kārikāsv a-dvaitā3khyaṃ tṛtīyaṃ prakaraṇam | oṃ
children.translated_text: Now, in the <s>Gauḍapādīya Kārikās</s>, the third chapter named <s>Advaita</s> (Non-duality). <s>Oṃ</s>.
The <s>dharma</s> that is dependent on meditation (<s>upāsanā</s>)
operates within the realm of the born <s>Brahman</s>;
before origination, everything is unborn (<s>aja</s>)—
therefore such a one is considered pitiable (<s>kṛpaṇa</s>).
Therefore I shall expound that which is free from pitiableness,
the unborn (<s>ajāti</s>), which has attained sameness;
how nothing whatsoever is born,
even though it appears to be born on all sides.
The <s>Ātman</s> is like space (<s>ākāśa</s>) with respect to the individual selves (<s>jīvas</s>),
as illustrated by the space within pots (<s>ghaṭākāśa</s>);
and like pots and the like with respect to aggregates—
this is the illustration regarding [apparent] birth.
When the pots and the like are dissolved,
the spaces within pots and so on,
merge into space itself—
so too do the <s>jīvas</s> merge into the <s>Ātman</s> here.
Just as when the space in one pot
becomes filled with dust, smoke, and the like,
not all [pot-spaces] become connected with them—
so too with the <s>jīvas</s> and pleasure and the like.
Forms, functions, and names
differ from place to place indeed,
but there is no differentiation of space—
such is the determination regarding the <s>jīvas</s>.
The pot-space (<s>ghaṭākāśa</s>) is not a modification
or a part of [universal] space—
likewise the <s>jīva</s> is never a modification
or a part of the <s>Ātman</s>.
Just as the sky appears to children
to be stained by impurities,
so too does the <s>Ātman</s> appear to the unwise
to be stained by impurities.
In death and in birth,
in going and in coming,
existing in all bodies,
[the <s>Ātman</s>] is not different from space.
All the aggregates, like dreams,
are projected by the <s>Ātman's</s> own <s>māyā</s> (illusion);
whether in superiority or in complete equality,
no rational justification is found [for their real origination].
The sheaths (<s>kośas</s>) beginning with <s>rasa</s> (the food-sheath),
which have been expounded in the <s>Taittirīyaka</s> (Taittirīya Upaniṣad),
of these, the <s>Ātman</s> is the supreme, the <s>jīva</s>—
thus it has been revealed, like space.
In the <s>Madhu</s> knowledge (of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad), regarding pairs,
the supreme <s>Brahman</s> is illuminated;
in the earth and in the body,
just as space is illuminated.
The non-difference of the <s>jīva</s> and the <s>Ātman</s>
is praised through their identity;
multiplicity is censured—
that [non-duality] alone is harmonious and consistent.
The separateness of <s>jīva</s> (individual self) and <s>ātman</s> (supreme Self)
that is declared as existing prior to origination—
that is figurative, spoken in the future tense;
a literal meaning is indeed not tenable.
The illustrations of clay, iron, sparks, and the like—
the creation that is taught through them and otherwise—
that is a means for introduction (to the teaching);
there is no real difference whatsoever.
The <s>āśramas</s> (stages of life) are threefold: of inferior,
middling, and superior vision.
This worship has been taught
for their sake, out of compassion.
Those who hold duality, firmly established
in the doctrinal positions of their own systems,
contradict one another;
but this (non-dual teaching) is not contradicted by them.
Non-duality (<s>advaita</s>) is indeed the ultimate reality;
duality is said to be its modification.
For them (the dualists), there is duality in both ways;
therefore, this (non-dual view) is not contradicted.
By <s>māyā</s> (illusion) indeed this (the unborn) is differentiated—
in no other way is the unborn (differentiated) whatsoever.
For if it were truly differentiated,
the immortal would become mortal.
Of that which is essentially unborn,
the disputants desire origination.
How can an unborn, immortal entity
arrive at mortality?
The immortal does not become mortal,
nor does the mortal become immortal likewise.
A change of one's essential nature
can never come about in any way.
For one whose entity is by nature immortal—
if that entity arrives at mortality,
how will the immortality produced by effort
remain steadfast for that one?
Whether created from what is real or from what is unreal—
the <s>śruti</s> (scripture) is equal regarding both.
That which is ascertained and supported by reasoning
is valid, and not the other.
"There is no plurality here" — from this scripture,
and also "<s>Indra</s> (appears) through <s>māyās</s> (illusory powers)";
"Though unborn, He is born in many ways"—
but He is born through <s>māyā</s> alone.

children.text: na iha nāna īti cā amnāyād

children.translated_text: By the negation of origination,
origination itself is denied;
"Who indeed could bring Him forth?"—
by this, the (notion of a) cause is denied.
"He, this (Self), is described as 'not this, not this'"—
since it negates everything that is predicated,
by virtue of being entirely ungraspable,
the unborn shines forth.

children.text: sa eṣa na iti na iti iti

children.translated_text: For what exists, birth through <s>māyā</s>
is tenable — but not in reality.
For one whose (entity) is truly born,
the already-born would be born again.
For what does not exist, birth through <s>māyā</s>
is not tenable even figuratively.
A barren woman's son is born
neither in reality nor through <s>māyā</s>.
Just as in dream the mind vibrates
with the appearance of duality, through <s>māyā</s>,
so too in the waking state, the mind vibrates
with the appearance of duality, through <s>māyā</s>.
The mind is non-dual yet appears as dual
in dream — of this there is no doubt.
The mind is non-dual yet appears as dual
likewise in waking — of this there is no doubt.
This entire duality, whatever there is,
moving and unmoving, is perceived by the mind.
For when the mind attains the state of no-mind,
duality is never apprehended.
When, through the realization of the truth of <s>ātman</s> (the Self),
one no longer engages in mental construction,
then the mind attains the state of no-mind,
in the absence of anything to be grasped, it becomes non-grasping.
Knowledge that is free from conceptualization, unborn,
and non-different from the knowable — thus they declare.
<s>Brahman</s> is the knowable, unborn, and eternal;
the unborn is realized by the unborn.
Of the restrained mind
of the wise one who is free from conceptualization—
that activity is to be understood;
it is different from that in deep sleep, and nothing else is equal to it.
In deep sleep, that (mind) is absorbed;
when restrained, it is not absorbed.
That itself is the fearless <s>Brahman</s>,
the light of knowledge in all directions.
Unborn, sleepless, dreamless,
nameless, formless,
shining once and for all, omniscient —
no figurative usage whatsoever applies.
Beyond all speech,
risen above all thought,
supremely peaceful, self-luminous,
<s>samādhi</s> — immovable and fearless.
There is neither grasping nor relinquishing there,
where no thought exists.
Then knowledge, established in the Self,
is unborn and has attained sameness.
<s>Asparśayoga</s> (the yoga of non-contact) is indeed its name —
it is difficult to perceive by all <s>yogins</s>.
For the <s>yogins</s> are afraid of it,
seeing fear where there is no fear.
Upon the restraint of the mind depends
the fearlessness of all <s>yogins</s>,
the destruction of suffering, awakening,
and imperishable peace itself.
Just as one might drain the ocean
drop by drop with the tip of a blade of <s>kuśa</s> grass,
so too the restraint of the mind
is achieved without weariness.
One should restrain by proper means
the mind distracted by desires and enjoyments.
Even when well-settled in torpor one should rouse it,
for torpor is the same as desire.
Remembering that all is suffering,
one should turn away from the enjoyment of desires.
Remembering that all is unborn,
one does not see anything as born.
One should awaken the mind when it lapses into torpor,
and pacify it again when distracted.
One should recognize it when it is tainted with attachment;
when it has attained equanimity, one should not disturb it.
One should not savour pleasure there;
through wisdom one should become detached.
The mind that is steady yet tends to wander —
one should unify it with effort.
When the mind neither lapses into torpor
nor is distracted again,
motionless and free from appearances —
that is <s>Brahman</s> then realized.
Self-abiding, peaceful, with <s>nirvāṇa</s>,
inexpressible, the supreme bliss —
unborn, known through the unborn knowable,
they call It the omniscient.
No individual soul (<s>jīva</s>) whatsoever is born;
there is no origination of it.
This is that supreme truth,
where nothing whatsoever is born.

children.text: iti (gauḍapādīya-kārikāyām a-dvaitā3khyaṃ [B:]gauḍapādīye āgama-śāstre '-dvaitā3khyaṃ) tṛtīyaṃ (prakaraṇam || oṃ tat sat || [B:]prakaraṇaṃ samāptam)
children.translated_text: Thus ends the third chapter called '<s>Advaita</s>' (Non-duality) in <s>Gauḍapāda's</s> <s>Āgamaśāstra</s>.
Now begins the fourth chapter called '<s>Alātaśānti</s>' (The Quenching of the Firebrand).
Through knowledge resembling space,
He who has perfectly awakened to <s>dharmas</s> that are like the sky,
non-different from the knowable —
to Him, the best among bipeds, I bow.
<s>Asparśayoga</s> (the yoga of non-contact) by name,
beneficial and conducive to the happiness of all beings,
free from dispute and contradiction —
that which has been taught, to it I pay homage.
Certain disputants desire the birth
of an existent entity indeed;
other wise ones, of a non-existent entity,
disputing amongst themselves.
Nothing existent is born;
nothing non-existent is born either.
By disputing thus, these dualists
actually proclaim non-origination (<s>ajāti</s>).
The non-origination (<s>ajāti</s>) proclaimed by them —
we approve of it.
We do not dispute with them;
know that which is free from dispute.
Of a <s>dharma</s> that is indeed unborn,
the disputants desire birth.
How can an unborn, immortal <s>dharma</s>
come to be subject to mortality?
The immortal does not become mortal,
nor [does] the mortal [become] immortal likewise.
The transformation of <s>prakṛti</s> (primordial nature) into something other
will never come about in any way.
One whose <s>dharma</s> is by its own nature immortal —
if it attains mortality,
how will that which is immortal by artifice
remain steady and unchanging?
That which is perfected, innate,
natural, and uncreated —
this should be known as <s>prakṛti</s> (nature),
which never abandons its own nature.
Free from old age and death
are all <s>dharmas</s> by their own nature.
Those who desire old age and death
fall away through that very thinking.
That for which the effect is the cause,
and the cause is born from it —
how can that which is being born be unborn?
And how can that which is divided be eternal?
If the effect is non-different from the cause,
then the effect is unborn;
for from an effect that is being born,
how can your cause be permanent?
For one who holds that something is born from the unborn,
there is indeed no example.
And from something already born giving rise to another,
an infinite regress follows.
For those who hold that the effect is the beginning of the cause
and the cause is the beginning of the effect —
how can beginninglessness of cause and effect
be described by them?
For those who hold that the effect is the beginning of the cause
and the cause is the beginning of the effect —
birth would be like theirs,
as the birth of a father from a son.
The sequence of cause and effect
must be sought by you;
for if they arise simultaneously,
there is no connection, like [two] horns [of an ox].
A cause arising from an effect —
your cause is not established.
How can an unestablished cause
produce an effect?
If the cause is established from the effect
and the effect is established from the cause,
which one came into being first,
upon whose establishment the other depends?
Inability, ignorance,
or disruption of sequence —
thus in every way by the wise
non-origination (<s>ajāti</s>) has been illuminated.
The illustration of the seed and sprout
is always equal to what is to be proved.
For an argument equal to what is to be proved
is not valid in establishing the thesis.
The non-comprehension of before and after
is itself the illumination of non-origination.
For from a <s>dharma</s> that is being born,
how is a prior [state] not apprehended?
From itself or from another,
nothing whatsoever is born.
Whether existent, non-existent, or both existent and non-existent —
nothing whatsoever is born.
The cause is not born, being beginningless;
and the effect too, by its very nature.
That which has no beginning —
for it, there is no origination.
Because designation has a cause,
otherwise both [subject and object] would perish;
from the apprehension of affliction,
the dependent (<s>paratantra</s>) existence is accepted.
Because designation has a cause,
this is accepted from the standpoint of reasoning.
The causelessness of the cause
is accepted from the standpoint of reality.
The mind does not touch the object,
nor the appearance of the object either.
Since the object is indeed unreal,
the appearance of the object is not separate from it.
The mind never touches a cause
in the three times.
Without a cause, error (<s>viparyāsa</s>)
how will it come to be for that [mind]?
Therefore the mind is not born,
nor are the objects perceived by the mind born.
Those who see their origination
indeed see a footprint in the sky.
Since the unborn is [said to be] born,
non-origination (<s>ajāti</s>) is its very nature (<s>prakṛti</s>);
the becoming-otherwise of [this] nature
will never come to be in any way.
That which is beginningless cannot have an end,
and <s>saṃsāra</s> will not be established [as such].
And that which has a beginning cannot be endless —
<s>mokṣa</s> (liberation) will not come to be [that way].
What does not exist at the beginning and at the end
is likewise [non-existent] in the present.
Though resembling unreal things,
they are perceived as if they were real.

children.text: ādāv ante ca yan na asti

children.translated_text: Their purposefulness
is contradicted in dream (variant: is also understood in dream).
Therefore, because of having a beginning and an end,
they are indeed rightly regarded as false.
All <s>dharmas</s> are false in dream,
as perceived within the body.
In this enclosed space indeed,
how can there be perception of [real] beings?
It is not reasonable to go [somewhere] and perceive,
since there is no regularity of time in the going.
And indeed everyone upon waking
does not exist in that [dream] place.
Having deliberated with friends and others,
upon awakening one does not encounter [them].
And whatever was grasped [in dream],
one does not see upon waking.
In dream the body is insubstantial,
since other [bodies] are also separately perceived.
Just as the body [in dream], so too is everything
perceived by the mind — insubstantial.
Because of apprehension, the waking state
is regarded as the cause of that [dream].
But because it is the cause of that [dream] alone,
the waking state is accepted as [equally] existent [or unreal].
Since origination is not established,
all is declared to be unborn.
And there is no arising whatsoever
of the non-existent from the existent.
Having seen the unreal in the waking state,
one sees [it again] in dream, absorbed in it.
Having seen the unreal also in dream,
upon waking one does not see [it].
The non-existent does not have a non-existent cause;
likewise, the existent does not have a non-existent cause.
The existent does not have an existent cause either;
how then could the non-existent have an existent cause?
Just as in the waking state, through error (<s>viparyāsa</s>),
one touches inconceivable things as if they were real,
so too in dream, through error,
one perceives <s>dharmas</s> right there [within the mind].
Because of apprehension and conventional practice,
for those who assert the reality of things —
birth has been taught by the <s>Buddhas</s>
always for those who are frightened of non-origination (<s>ajāti</s>).
For those frightened of non-origination,
who deviate due to [mere] apprehension —
the defects of [asserting] birth will not apply,
and only a small defect will remain.
Because of apprehension and conventional practice,
a magical elephant is so called;
because of apprehension and conventional practice,
an [existing] thing is likewise so called.
The appearance of birth, the appearance of movement,
and likewise the appearance of things —
[in reality there is] non-birth, non-movement, non-thingness:
<s>vijñāna</s> (consciousness) is peaceful and non-dual.
Thus the mind is not born;
thus all <s>dharmas</s> are regarded as unborn.
Those who know thus
do not fall into error (<s>viparyāsa</s>).
Just as a whirling firebrand (<s>alāta</s>) appears
as straight, curved, and so forth,
so the vibration of consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>)
appears as apprehender and apprehended.
Just as the firebrand (<s>alāta</s>) when not whirling
is without appearances and unborn,
Consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>) is unmoving,
without appearance, and likewise unborn.
When the firebrand (<s>alāta</s>) is moving, indeed,
the appearances do not come from elsewhere;
nor from that [firebrand] when it is motionless do they go elsewhere —
they do not enter into the firebrand.
They have not come out of the firebrand,
because they lack the nature of substance (<s>dravyatva</s>).
In the case of consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>) too, it would be just the same,
because there is no difference regarding the appearances.
When consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>) is moving, indeed,
the appearances do not come from elsewhere;
nor from that [consciousness] when it is motionless do they go elsewhere —
they do not enter into consciousness.
They have not come out of consciousness,
because they lack the nature of substance.
Since there is no relation of cause and effect,
they are always inconceivable.
A substance could be the cause of a substance,
and one thing indeed the cause of another.
But substance-hood or otherness
of <s>dharmas</s> (phenomena) is not tenable.
Thus, <s>dharmas</s> are not born from mind,
nor is mind born from <s>dharmas</s>.
Thus, the wise enter into
the non-origination of cause and effect.
As long as there is involvement with cause and effect,
so long is there the arising of cause and effect.
When involvement with cause and effect ceases,
there is no arising of cause and effect.
As long as there is involvement with cause and effect,
<s>saṃsāra</s> (the cycle of existence) extends that long.
When involvement with cause and effect ceases,
one does not enter into <s>saṃsāra</s>.
From the conventional standpoint (<s>saṃvṛti</s>), everything is born;
therefore, nothing is eternal.
By its own nature (<s>svabhāva</s>), everything is indeed unborn;
therefore, there is no annihilation.

children.text: śāśvataṃ (na asti tena [B:]tena na asti) vai

children.translated_text: The <s>dharmas</s> that appear to be born —
they are not born in reality (<s>tattva</s>).
Their birth is like an illusion (<s>māyā</s>),
and that <s>māyā</s> itself does not exist.
Just as from a seed made of illusion (<s>māyā</s>)
a sprout of the same nature is born —
it is neither permanent nor subject to annihilation;
the same reasoning applies to <s>dharmas</s>.

children.text: na asau nityo na ca ucchedī

children.translated_text: With regard to all <s>dharmas</s> that are unborn,
the designation of eternal or non-eternal does not apply.
Where words do not operate,
discrimination cannot be spoken of.
Just as in dream, the mind appears as duality
and moves through <s>māyā</s> (illusion),
so too in waking, the mind appears as duality
and moves through <s>māyā</s>.
Non-dual yet appearing as duality —
the mind in dream, there is no doubt.
Non-dual yet appearing as duality —
so too in waking, there is no doubt.
The dreamer, wandering in the dream,
sees beings situated in the ten directions —
those born from eggs and those born from sweat —
the living beings (<s>jīvas</s>) that he always perceives.
Those are merely perceived by the dreamer's mind;
they do not exist apart from it.
Likewise, all this is merely the seen,
and is accepted as the dreamer's mind alone.
The waking person, moving about in the waking state,
sees beings situated in the ten directions —
those born from eggs and those born from sweat —
the living beings (<s>jīvas</s>) that he always perceives.
Those are merely objects perceived by the waking mind;
they do not exist apart from it.
Likewise, all this is merely the seen,
and is accepted as the waking mind alone.
Both [dream and waking] are mutually perceived by each other —
what can be said to truly exist?
Both are devoid of distinguishing characteristics;
each is grasped only by its own theory.

children.text: kiṃ tad asti iti ca ucyate

children.translated_text: Just as a dream-born being (<s>jīva</s>)
is born and also dies,
so too all these beings
come into existence and cease to exist.
Just as an illusion-born being (<s>jīva</s>)
is born and also dies,
so too all these beings
they exist and they do not exist.
Just as a magically created being
is born and also dies,
so too all these <s>jīvas</s> (individual souls)
exist and do not exist.
No <s>jīva</s> (individual soul) is ever born;
there is no origination of it.
This is the supreme truth:
nothing whatsoever is born.
This entire [duality of] grasped and grasper
is but the vibration of the mind.
The mind is eternally without an object,
therefore it is declared to be unattached.
That which exists by imagined convention (<s>kalpitasaṃvṛti</s>)
does not exist in the ultimate sense (<s>paramārtha</s>).
By dependent convention (<s>paratantrābhisaṃvṛti</s>) [Variant B: the dependent one, by convention]
it may exist, but not ultimately.
The unborn (<s>aja</s>) by imagined convention,
is not even unborn in the ultimate sense;
by dependent origination (<s>paratantrābhiniṣpatti</s>) [Variant B: the dependent one, by origination],
it is born only conventionally.
There is clinging to the unreal;
duality does not exist therein.
Having realized the absence of duality,
one who is without cause is not born.
When one does not find causes —
superior, inferior, or middling —
then the mind is not born;
in the absence of a cause, whence the effect?
Of the causeless mind,
the non-arising is equal and non-dual.
Since everything is indeed unborn,
the visible world is but [a projection of] the mind.
Having realized the true causelessness [of all things],
not finding any separate cause, [Variant B: not finding]
one attains the state free from sorrow, free from desire, [Variant B: then, free from desire]
and free from fear.
Due to clinging to the unreal,
the mind functions as if [objects] were real.
Having realized the non-existence of things,
it withdraws, free from attachment.
Of the one who has ceased and does not engage,
the state is then truly unwavering.
That is the domain of the <s>Buddhas</s> (awakened ones) —
that sameness, unborn and non-dual.
Unborn, without sleep, without dream,
it shines forth of itself.
For this <s>dharma</s> is self-luminous once and for all,
by the very nature of [its] essence (<s>dhātu</s>). [Variant B: the essence, by its own nature]
Happiness is always concealed,
and suffering is always revealed.
Of whatsoever <s>dharma</s>,
that Blessed One is [realized] through [its] apprehension.
"It exists, it does not exist, it exists, it does not exist,"
or again, "it does not exist, it does not exist" —
through [views of] moving, stationary, both, or neither —
the childish one merely conceals [the truth].

children.text: asti na asty asti na asti iti
na asti na asti iti vā punaḥ

children.translated_text: These are the four positions (<s>koṭi</s>),
by whose grasp one is always enveloped. [Variant K: enveloped together with]
The Blessed One is untouched by these;
by whom He is seen, that one is the all-seer.
Having attained complete omniscience
and the non-dual state of <s>Brahman</s> (<s>brāhmaṇya</s>),
that which has no beginning, middle, or end —
what more could one desire beyond this?
This is the discipline of the <s>Brāhmaṇas</s> (the wise) —
tranquility (<s>śama</s>) is said to be natural;
self-control (<s>dama</s>) comes from being naturally subdued —
thus the knower should enter into peace.
With substance and with apprehension —
duality is accepted as worldly.
Without substance but with apprehension —
this is accepted as purified worldly [knowledge].
Without substance and without apprehension —
this is held to be supramundane (<s>lokottara</s>).
Knowledge, the knowable, and that which is to be fully known —
these are always proclaimed by the <s>Buddhas</s>.
When the threefold knowable in knowledge
is known sequentially by oneself,
omniscience in all respects
arises here for the one of great intellect.
That which is to be avoided, that which is to be known, that which is to be attained, and that which is to be purified —
should be known from the foremost [standpoint].
Apart from them [i.e., the dharmas], one should know that
apprehension (<s>upalambha</s>) is declared to be in the three [states].
All <s>dharmas</s>, beginningless by nature,
should be known as like <s>ākāśa</s> (space).
For there is no plurality whatsoever
among them, in any way, anywhere.
All <s>dharmas</s> are firmly established
as awakened from the very beginning by their own nature.
Whoever has such patient acceptance (<s>kṣānti</s>),
that one is fit for immortality (<s>amṛtatva</s>).
Peaceful from the beginning, unborn,
by their very nature completely quiescent (<s>sunirvṛta</s>) —
all <s>dharmas</s> are equally non-differentiated,
unborn, uniform, and clear.
Clarity (<s>vaiśāradya</s>) indeed does not exist
for those who always move about in differentiation.
Inclined toward differentiation, proponents of multiplicity —
therefore they are called pitiable.
But those who will become
firmly established in the unborn and the uniform,
they are the ones of great knowledge in the world,
and the world does not fathom that.
In unborn <s>dharmas</s>, knowledge is held to be
unborn and non-transferring.
Since knowledge does not pass over [to objects],
it is therefore proclaimed as unattached (<s>asaṅga</s>).
If even the slightest difference
arises, the unwise [would find that]
non-attachment never exists —
how much less the removal of the covering?
All <s>dharmas</s> have never acquired a covering;
they are pure by nature.
Awakened from the beginning and likewise liberated —
they are awakened, thus [declare] the leaders.
The knowledge of the <s>Buddha</s>
does not pass over to <s>dharmas</s>, the protector's [knowledge].
All <s>dharmas</s> and likewise knowledge —
this was not taught by the <s>Buddha</s>.
Hard to see and exceedingly profound,
unborn, uniform, and clear —
having realized the state of non-plurality,
we bow down as best we can.

children.text: iti (gauḍa-pādā3cārya-kṛtā māṇḍūkyo1paniṣad-kārikāḥ saṃpūrṇāḥ [B:]gauḍapādīye āgama-śāstre 'lāta-śānty-ākhyaṃ caturthaṃ prakaraṇaṃ samāptam)
children.translated_text: Thus ends the <s>Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad Kārikās</s> composed by <s>Ācārya Gauḍapāda</s> [Variant: Thus ends the fourth chapter called <s>Alātaśānti</s> (Quenching of the Firebrand) in the <s>Āgamaśāstra</s> by <s>Gauḍapāda</s>].
